entries.meaning: An informal word for a mother. ---
examples: My mom picks the kids up on Tuesdays.
Ask your mom if you can stay for dinner.
A group of moms organized the whole fundraiser.
entries.contrast: Americans say mom; the British say mum.

entries.meaning: An informal word for a father. ---
examples: Her dad coaches the soccer team.
I stayed home with my dad while Mom traveled.
The dads took turns driving to practice.

entries.meaning: A child's affectionate word for a mother. ---
examples: Mommy, can I have some juice?
She cried for her mommy the whole first day of school.
All the mommies stood at the classroom door.
entries.contrast: British children say mummy.

entries.meaning: A child's affectionate word for a father. ---
examples: Daddy, watch me jump!
He fell asleep on his daddy's shoulder.
The daddies were all in the kitchen doing dishes.

entries.meaning: An informal word for a grandmother. ---
examples: We spend every Thanksgiving at Grandma's house.
My grandma taught me how to make pie crust.
Both grandmas came to the birthday party.
entries.contrast: The d is not pronounced — grandma comes out as GRAN-mah.

entries.meaning: An informal word for a grandfather. ---
examples: Grandpa let me steer the boat.
Her grandpa still drives himself to church.
The kids have four grandpas between them.

entries.meaning: An object made for a child to play with. ---
examples: He got a new toy for finishing his chores.
Please put your toys away before dinner.
The living room floor is covered in toys.

entries.meaning: A small model of a person that a child plays with. ---
examples: She carries that doll everywhere.
He fed the doll pretend soup.
Her dolls are lined up along the windowsill.

entries.meaning: The work of raising a child. ---
examples: Good parenting takes a lot of patience.
They disagree about parenting almost every day.
She writes a parenting column for the paper.

entries.meaning: The work of looking after children while their parents are away. ---
examples: Childcare costs more than their rent.
We could not find childcare for the summer.
Her company offers on-site childcare.
entries.русский: уход за детьми, присмотр за ребёнком
entries.contrast: Written either solid, childcare, or as two words, child care.

entries.meaning: Someone employed to look after a family's children. ---
examples: They hired a nanny when the twins were born.
Our nanny takes the kids to the park every morning.
Two nannies were chatting by the swings.

entries.meaning: Someone who watches a child for a few hours while the parents are out. ---
examples: We need a sitter for Friday night.
The sitter put them to bed at eight.
Good sitters book up weeks in advance.

entries.meaning: The job of watching someone's children for a short time. ---
examples: She earns extra money babysitting.
Babysitting pays fifteen dollars an hour around here.
He gave up babysitting once he got a real job.

entries.meaning: A young person between about thirteen and nineteen. ---
examples: Raising a teen is nothing like raising a toddler.
The movie is aimed at teens.
Most teens here have a part-time job.

entries.meaning: A friendly, informal word for a child. ---
examples: Nice job, kiddo.
How was school, kiddo?
She packed lunches for all three kiddos.

entries.meaning: A very small child. ---
examples: A tot in rain boots splashed through the puddle.
The library runs a story hour for tots.
Half the tots fell asleep on the bus.

entries.meaning: A child or young teenager. ---
examples: The coach is great with youngsters.
One youngster raised his hand for every question.
Local youngsters cleaned up the riverbank.

entries.meaning: A child of about three or four, too young for regular school. ---
examples: A preschooler asks about a hundred questions a day.
The class is designed for preschoolers.
Our preschooler still naps in the afternoon.

entries.meaning: A child in the school year before first grade. ---
examples: My kindergartener lost his second tooth today.
The kindergarteners sang two songs at the assembly.
Every kindergartener gets a nap mat.

entries.meaning: A child with no brothers or sisters. ---
examples: He grew up an only child in a quiet house.
Being an only child has its advantages.
Both of my parents were only children.
entries.contrast: Irregular plural: only children, never "only childs".

entries.meaning: The oldest child in a family. ---
examples: Their firstborn just turned nine.
As the firstborn, she got stuck babysitting.
Firstborns often end up bossy.

entries.meaning: One of three children born at the same birth. ---
examples: One triplet was born much smaller than the others.
They have triplets and a dog.
The triplets wore matching hats.

entries.meaning: The husband of your mother, who is not your birth father. ---
examples: Her stepfather taught her to drive.
He gets along fine with his stepfather.
Both stepfathers came to the graduation.

entries.meaning: The child of your husband or wife from an earlier relationship. ---
examples: He raised his stepchild as his own.
She has two stepchildren in high school.
The stepchildren stay with us every other weekend.
entries.contrast: Irregular plural: stepchildren, like children.

entries.meaning: A woman who promises at a baptism to help raise a child. ---
examples: My aunt is also my godmother.
The godmother held the baby at the font.
Both godmothers flew in for the christening.

entries.meaning: Godfather has 3 distinct senses.
examples: He asked his oldest friend to be the godfather.
Her godfather sends a card every birthday.
The godfathers stood on the left side of the altar.
Prosecutors named him as the godfather of the city's crime family.
Two godfathers met to divide up the territory.
Agents spent years building a case against the godfather.
He's often called the godfather of hip-hop.
Those two are the godfathers of modern stand-up.
She thanked the godfather of the genre in her acceptance speech.

senses.head: A man who promises at a baptism to help raise a child
examples: He asked his oldest friend to be the godfather.
Her godfather sends a card every birthday.
The godfathers stood on the left side of the altar.

senses.head: The head of a Mafia family or other crime organization
examples: Prosecutors named him as the godfather of the city's crime family.
Two godfathers met to divide up the territory.
Agents spent years building a case against the godfather.

senses.head: A man seen as the founder or leading early figure of a movement or style
examples: He's often called the godfather of hip-hop.
Those two are the godfathers of modern stand-up.
She thanked the godfather of the genre in her acceptance speech.

entries.русский: крёстный отец; крёстный отец (глава мафиозного клана); основоположник, отец (направления, жанра)

entries.meaning: A child who regularly plays with another child. ---
examples: The boy next door is his favorite playmate.
She needs a playmate her own age.
The two playmates built a fort out of couch cushions.

entries.meaning: A badly behaved or spoiled child. ---
examples: He was acting like a total brat in the store.
Nobody wants to raise a brat.
The restaurant was full of screaming brats.

entries.meaning: A young foreigner who lives with a family and helps with the children. ---
examples: Their au pair is from Germany.
We host an au pair for a year at a time.
The au pairs meet up downtown on weekends.
entries.русский: о-пэр, помощница по хозяйству из другой страны
entries.contrast: From French, but said the English way: oh-PAIR.

entries.meaning: Caretaker has 2 distinct senses.
examples: A child needs at least one steady caretaker.
She became the main caretaker for both kids.
The caretakers rotate on a weekly schedule.
The caretaker plows the driveway and keeps the pipes from freezing.
We left a key with the caretaker of the cabin.
Two caretakers mow the cemetery every week.

senses.head: Someone who looks after a person who cannot look after themselves
examples: A child needs at least one steady caretaker.
She became the main caretaker for both kids.
The caretakers rotate on a weekly schedule.

senses.head: A person paid to look after a building or piece of land
examples: The caretaker plows the driveway and keeps the pipes from freezing.
We left a key with the caretaker of the cabin.
Two caretakers mow the cemetery every week.

entries.русский: тот, кто ухаживает (за ребёнком, больным); смотритель, сторож (здания, участка)
entries.contrast: In American English a caretaker looks after people; in British English it is the janitor of a building.

entries.meaning: A doctor who cares for women during pregnancy and birth. ---
examples: Her obstetrician wants to see her every week now.
We switched obstetricians halfway through.
The obstetrician met us at the hospital at 3 a.m.

entries.meaning: The state of being a parent. ---
examples: Nothing prepares you for parenthood.
They eased into parenthood slowly.
Parenthood changed how he spends his weekends.

entries.meaning: The state of being a father. ---
examples: Fatherhood suits him.
He talks about fatherhood like it saved his life.
The book is about first-year fatherhood.

entries.meaning: The stage of life when a person is a baby. ---
examples: She barely remembers his babyhood — it went so fast.
The photos cover his whole babyhood.
He was sick through most of babyhood.

entries.meaning: The stage of life between about one and three years old. ---
examples: Toddlerhood is exhausting and wonderful.
We survived toddlerhood on coffee.
Tantrums are normal in toddlerhood.
entries.русский: ранний возраст (примерно от года до трёх)

entries.meaning: The period when a child's body changes into an adult's. ---
examples: He hit puberty the summer after sixth grade.
Kids reach puberty earlier than they used to.
Puberty explains a lot about her moods lately.

entries.meaning: A padded safety seat that straps a small child into a car. ---
examples: You cannot leave the hospital without a car seat.
He fell asleep in his car seat before we hit the highway.
Both car seats barely fit across the back row.
entries.contrast: In American usage a car seat is almost always the child's safety seat, not just any seat in a car.

entries.meaning: A small basket-like bed for a newborn baby. ---
examples: The bassinet fits right next to our bed.
She outgrew the bassinet in two months.
The hospital lines the bassinets up along the window.

entries.meaning: A small fenced area where a baby can play safely. ---
examples: I put him in the playpen while I cooked.
The playpen folds up for travel.
Both playpens are set up in the basement.

entries.meaning: A device that lets parents hear or see a baby in another room. ---
examples: Turn the baby monitor up so we can hear her.
The baby monitor picked up the neighbor's TV.
Video baby monitors have gotten cheap.

entries.meaning: A bag for carrying a baby's diapers, wipes, and supplies. ---
examples: Grab the diaper bag before we go.
There is a change of clothes in the diaper bag.
Their diaper bags were stuffed with snacks.

entries.meaning: A waist-high table where a baby's diaper is changed. ---
examples: Never walk away from the changing table.
The changing table has drawers underneath.
Most restrooms here have changing tables.

entries.meaning: A barrier across a doorway or stairs to keep a small child out. ---
examples: Put the baby gate back up at the top of the stairs.
He figured out how to open the baby gate.
We have baby gates on both floors.

entries.meaning: Bouncer has 2 distinct senses.
examples: She naps best in the bouncer.
Set the bouncer on the floor, never on a table.
Both bouncers came from a garage sale.
The bouncer checked our IDs at the door.
Two bouncers walked the drunk guy outside.
He worked as a bouncer while he was in college.

senses.head: A soft springy seat that rocks a baby up and down
examples: She naps best in the bouncer.
Set the bouncer on the floor, never on a table.
Both bouncers came from a garage sale.

senses.head: A strong man employed by a bar or club to keep out or throw out troublemakers
examples: The bouncer checked our IDs at the door.
Two bouncers walked the drunk guy outside.
He worked as a bouncer while he was in college.

entries.русский: детский шезлонг-качалка; вышибала, охранник в клубе
entries.contrast: The same word also means the man who throws people out of a bar.

entries.meaning: Walker has 3 distinct senses.
examples: He raced across the kitchen in his walker.
Doctors here discourage the use of a walker.
Old-style walkers are banned in Canada.
She gets around the house with a walker.
After the hip surgery he needed a walker for a month.
The hallway is wide enough for two walkers to pass.
The trail is popular with walkers and runners.
Early-morning walkers filled the park.
She's a fast walker, so I had trouble keeping up.

senses.head: A wheeled frame with a seat that a baby scoots around in
examples: He raced across the kitchen in his walker.
Doctors here discourage the use of a walker.
Old-style walkers are banned in Canada.

senses.head: A metal frame that a person leans on for support while walking
examples: She gets around the house with a walker.
After the hip surgery he needed a walker for a month.
The hallway is wide enough for two walkers to pass.

senses.head: A person who is walking, especially for exercise
examples: The trail is popular with walkers and runners.
Early-morning walkers filled the park.
She's a fast walker, so I had trouble keeping up.

entries.русский: ходунки (детские); ходунки (для пожилых, больных); пешеход, любитель ходьбы
entries.contrast: Russian ходунки is plural, but English uses a singular: a walker.

entries.meaning: Sling has 2 distinct senses.
examples: She wore the baby in a sling all afternoon.
The sling leaves both hands free.
Fabric slings are easier on your back than you would think.
She had her arm in a sling for a month.
The sling keeps the shoulder from moving.
The clinic gave out slings and ice packs.

senses.head: A wide cloth loop worn over the shoulder to carry a baby
examples: She wore the baby in a sling all afternoon.
The sling leaves both hands free.
Fabric slings are easier on your back than you would think.

senses.head: A cloth loop worn around the neck to support an injured arm
examples: She had her arm in a sling for a month.
The sling keeps the shoulder from moving.
The clinic gave out slings and ice packs.

entries.русский: слинг, перевязь для ношения ребёнка; перевязь для руки, косыночная повязка

entries.meaning: A rubber nipple a baby sucks on for comfort. ---
examples: The pacifier fell out and he woke right up.
We are trying to take away the pacifier this month.
There are three pacifiers somewhere in that crib.
entries.contrast: American pacifier, British dummy.

entries.meaning: A casual word for a baby's pacifier. ---
examples: Where did his binky go?
She will not sleep without the binky.
We keep spare binkies in every room.

entries.meaning: Rattle has 2 distinct senses.
examples: He shook the rattle and laughed.
The rattle rolled under the couch.
Wooden rattles were a popular shower gift.
There's a rattle under the hood at low speeds.
The wind set up a rattle in the storm door.
I keep hearing a rattle somewhere in the dashboard.

senses.head: A baby's toy that makes a noise when it is shaken
examples: He shook the rattle and laughed.
The rattle rolled under the couch.
Wooden rattles were a popular shower gift.

senses.head: A quick series of short knocking sounds
examples: There's a rattle under the hood at low speeds.
The wind set up a rattle in the storm door.
I keep hearing a rattle somewhere in the dashboard.

entries.meaning: A soft object a baby chews on while teeth are coming in. ---
examples: Keep the teether in the freezer.
He gnawed on the teether for an hour.
Silicone teethers are easy to clean.

entries.meaning: A ring-shaped teether that a baby can grip and chew. ---
examples: She dropped the teething ring on the floor again.
A cold teething ring calms him down fast.
We went through four teething rings that winter.

entries.meaning: A soft toy bear that a child sleeps with or carries around. ---
examples: He will not go anywhere without that teddy bear.
The teddy bear has been washed so many times it is gray.
Her shelf is crowded with teddy bears.

entries.meaning: A soft toy shaped like an animal. ---
examples: She lined up every stuffed animal along the wall.
He won a stuffed animal at the fair.
The stuffed animals take up half the bed.
entries.contrast: Americans say stuffed animal; the British say soft toy or cuddly toy.

entries.meaning: A blanket a small child carries around for comfort. ---
examples: He drags that security blanket through the whole house.
We had to sneak the security blanket into the wash.
Some kids never have security blankets at all.

entries.meaning: A sealed bin for used diapers. ---
examples: Somebody needs to empty the diaper pail.
The diaper pail keeps the smell down surprisingly well.
We have diaper pails in both bedrooms.

entries.meaning: A device a mother uses to draw milk from her breasts. ---
examples: Insurance covered most of the breast pump.
She keeps a breast pump at the office.
Electric breast pumps are much faster.
entries.contrast: The ea in breast is short: BREST, not "breest".

entries.meaning: A machine that kills germs on bottles and pacifiers with steam. ---
examples: Run the bottles through the sterilizer.
The sterilizer takes about eight minutes.
Countertop sterilizers were on every registry.

entries.meaning: A small lamp left on so a child is not in the dark. ---
examples: He will not sleep without a nightlight.
The nightlight burned out and she panicked.
We put nightlights in the hallway too.

entries.meaning: Damp disposable cloths for cleaning a baby. ---
examples: We are out of baby wipes again.
Baby wipes clean up just about anything.
Keep a pack of baby wipes in the glove box.
entries.contrast: Almost always used in the plural, even for one pack.

entries.meaning: A thick ointment put on a baby's bottom to prevent soreness. ---
examples: Put some diaper cream on before you close it up.
We ran out of diaper cream on the second day of the trip.
That diaper cream cleared it up overnight.

entries.meaning: Thick underwear worn by a child learning to use the toilet. ---
examples: He wears training pants to preschool now.
Training pants catch the small accidents.
Pack an extra pair of training pants.
entries.contrast: Plural only, like pants — one item is "a pair of training pants".

entries.meaning: A one-piece baby garment that snaps between the legs. ---
examples: She spit up on her third onesie today.
That onesie says "Daddy's Little Helper."
We got a dozen onesies at the shower.
entries.contrast: Spelled with one e in the middle but said WUN-zee, from one.

entries.meaning: A loose one-piece outfit with short legs, worn by small children. ---
examples: He wore a striped romper to the picnic.
That romper is already too short in the legs.
Summer rompers are the easiest thing to change him in.
entries.русский: песочник, детский комбинезон с короткими штанинами

entries.meaning: A snug wrap that holds a baby's arms tucked in. ---
examples: A tight swaddle is the only thing that settles her.
He wriggled out of the swaddle by midnight.
We bought two zip-up swaddles.

entries.meaning: A small cloth put over the shoulder to catch what a baby spits up. ---
examples: Throw a burp cloth over your shoulder first.
That burp cloth has seen better days.
There are clean burp cloths in the second drawer.

entries.meaning: A low bed with side rails, used after a child outgrows the crib. ---
examples: We moved him into a toddler bed at two.
The toddler bed uses the same crib mattress.
Both toddler beds came from the same store.

entries.meaning: The work of making a home safe for a small child. ---
examples: Childproofing took an entire weekend.
We did the childproofing right before he started crawling.
Childproofing means locks on every low cabinet.

entries.meaning: The milk a mother's body makes to feed her baby. ---
examples: Breast milk keeps four days in the fridge.
She freezes extra breast milk in small bags.
He gets breast milk at night and formula during the day.

entries.meaning: Feeding a baby with milk from the mother's breast. ---
examples: Breastfeeding was harder than she expected.
The hospital has a class on breastfeeding.
She stopped breastfeeding at ten months.

entries.meaning: Nursing has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Nursing every two hours wore her out.
She found a quiet room for nursing.
Nursing got easier after the first month.
She's going back to school for nursing.
Twenty years of nursing taught him patience.
The hospital has a serious nursing shortage.

senses.head: Feeding a baby at the breast
examples: Nursing every two hours wore her out.
She found a quiet room for nursing.
Nursing got easier after the first month.

senses.head: The profession of caring for sick and injured people
examples: She's going back to school for nursing.
Twenty years of nursing taught him patience.
The hospital has a serious nursing shortage.

entries.русский: кормление грудью; сестринское дело, профессия медсестры
entries.contrast: The same word also means the profession of a nurse — context decides.

entries.meaning: Air coming up loudly from the stomach through the mouth. ---
examples: Wait for a burp before you lay her down.
That was a big burp for such a little guy.
Two good burps and he was fine.

entries.meaning: The small amount of milk a baby brings back up after feeding. ---
examples: There is spit-up on your collar.
A little spit-up after every bottle is normal.
The spit-up came right out of the shirt.
entries.contrast: The noun is hyphenated, spit-up; the verb is two words, spit up.

entries.meaning: Soft mashed food made for babies who cannot chew yet. ---
examples: She makes her own baby food in a blender.
The jars of baby food are on aisle six.
He spat the baby food straight back out.

entries.meaning: Real food, as opposed to milk, given to a baby starting to eat. ---
examples: We started solids at six months.
He is not interested in solids yet.
The doctor said to introduce solids one at a time.
entries.contrast: In this baby-feeding sense the word is always plural: solids.

entries.meaning: The process of moving a baby off breast or bottle onto other food. ---
examples: Weaning went more smoothly than we feared.
She started weaning around a year.
Slow weaning is easier on everyone.

entries.meaning: Long spells of crying in a healthy baby, often in the evening. ---
examples: The doctor said it was just colic.
Colic had us up every night for two months.
Nothing helps colic except time.

entries.meaning: A condition where stomach contents come back up the throat. ---
examples: The baby has reflux, so we keep her upright after meals.
Reflux usually settles down by six months.
They put him on medicine for the reflux.

entries.meaning: The period when a baby's first teeth push through the gums. ---
examples: Teething has him drooling all day.
She blamed the fussiness on teething.
Teething pain is worst at night.

entries.meaning: Time a baby spends lying face down to build neck and arm strength. ---
examples: He hates tummy time but it is good for him.
Do a few minutes of tummy time after every nap.
Tummy time helps them learn to roll over.

entries.meaning: A short period when a child grows unusually fast. ---
examples: He is eating like crazy — must be a growth spurt.
She went up two shoe sizes in one growth spurt.
Growth spurts mess up their sleep for a week.

entries.meaning: The part of the day set aside for a small child to sleep. ---
examples: Do not call between one and three — that is naptime.
We moved naptime an hour later.
Naptime is sacred in this house.

entries.meaning: Teaching a baby to fall asleep alone and stay asleep. ---
examples: We tried sleep training at seven months.
Sleep training was three rough nights and then peace.
Not everyone believes in sleep training.

entries.meaning: The practice of a baby sleeping in the parents' bed or room. ---
examples: Co-sleeping got us through the first year.
Their pediatrician warned them about co-sleeping.
Co-sleeping is much more common in other countries.

entries.meaning: An episode in which a sleeping child screams but does not wake up. ---
examples: He had a night terror around eleven o'clock.
During a night terror you cannot really comfort them.
The night terrors stopped when he turned five.
entries.contrast: Not the same as a nightmare — a child having a night terror stays asleep.

entries.meaning: Wetting the bed during sleep, common in young children. ---
examples: Bedwetting is normal well past age five.
They put a plastic sheet down because of the bedwetting.
The doctor said not to punish him for bedwetting.

entries.meaning: Babble has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Her babble is starting to sound like sentences.
We heard happy babble through the monitor.
That babble turns into words faster than you think.
A babble of voices filled the hallway.
I couldn't hear the announcement over the babble.
The room went from a babble to total silence.

senses.head: The repeated sounds a baby makes before real words
examples: Her babble is starting to sound like sentences.
We heard happy babble through the monitor.
That babble turns into words faster than you think.

senses.head: A confused noise of many people talking at once
examples: A babble of voices filled the hallway.
I couldn't hear the announcement over the babble.
The room went from a babble to total silence.

entries.meaning: The first walking a baby does without help. ---
examples: She took her first steps in the kitchen.
We missed his first steps — the sitter saw them.
Most babies take their first steps around a year.
entries.contrast: Nearly always plural: you take your first steps, not "your first step".

entries.meaning: A chart the doctor uses to track a child's height and weight. ---
examples: He is off the top of the growth chart.
The nurse plotted her on the growth chart.
Growth charts differ a little from country to country.

entries.meaning: The first set of teeth, which fall out in childhood. ---
examples: He has lost four baby teeth already.
Baby teeth still need brushing twice a day.
Kids get twenty baby teeth in all.
entries.contrast: Irregular: one baby tooth, several baby teeth. The British say milk teeth.

entries.meaning: An imaginary figure who leaves money for a child's lost tooth. ---
examples: Put it under your pillow for the tooth fairy.
The tooth fairy forgot to come last night.
In this house the tooth fairy pays a dollar.

entries.meaning: The soft gap in a baby's skull where the bones have not joined yet. ---
examples: Be careful of the soft spot on the top of his head.
The soft spot closed up by fourteen months.
Newborns have two soft spots, front and back.
entries.contrast: Also used figuratively: to have a soft spot for someone is to be fond of them.

entries.meaning: Flaky yellow crust on a baby's scalp. ---
examples: That patch on his head is just cradle cap.
Olive oil loosens up cradle cap.
Cradle cap looks worse than it is.

entries.meaning: Red sore skin where a baby's diaper sits. ---
examples: She has a bad diaper rash this week.
Change him more often and the diaper rash will clear.
Diaper rashes flare up whenever he is teething.

entries.meaning: A shot that protects a child against a disease. ---
examples: The school needs a record of every immunization.
He gets two immunizations at this visit.
Immunization rates dropped that year.
entries.contrast: American spelling immunization; the British write immunisation.

entries.meaning: A childhood illness that gives a harsh barking cough. ---
examples: That barking cough is croup.
Croup always seems to start at two in the morning.
Steam from the shower helps with croup.
entries.contrast: Rhymes with soup, not with cup.

entries.meaning: Aches in a child's legs at night during periods of fast growth. ---
examples: He woke up crying with growing pains.
Growing pains usually hit in the calves.
A warm bath eases the growing pains.
entries.contrast: Plural only, and also used figuratively for a young company's early troubles.

entries.meaning: The habit of putting the thumb in the mouth for comfort. ---
examples: The dentist warned us about thumb sucking.
Thumb sucking is how she falls asleep.
He gave up thumb sucking on his own.
entries.contrast: The b in thumb is silent: THUM.

entries.meaning: A child who refuses most foods. ---
examples: My youngest is a real picky eater.
Cooking for a picky eater is exhausting.
Most picky eaters grow out of it.

entries.meaning: A child's distress at being away from a parent. ---
examples: Separation anxiety usually peaks around nine months.
Drop-off is hard because of the separation anxiety.
She outgrew the separation anxiety by preschool.

entries.meaning: The stage around age two when a child says no to everything. ---
examples: We are deep in the terrible twos.
The terrible twos hit her early.
Everyone warns you about the terrible twos.
entries.contrast: Always plural and always with the: the terrible twos.

entries.meaning: Jealousy and competition between brothers and sisters. ---
examples: Sibling rivalry got worse after the baby came.
A little sibling rivalry is normal.
They fight, but it is ordinary sibling rivalry.

entries.meaning: A pretend companion a young child talks to and plays with. ---
examples: She set a place at the table for her imaginary friend.
His imaginary friend is named Bobo.
Imaginary friends are a sign of a good imagination.

entries.meaning: The day a baby is expected to be born. ---
examples: Her due date is the fourth of March.
He came two weeks after the due date.
Due dates are really just estimates.

entries.meaning: A scan that shows a picture of a baby inside the womb. ---
examples: We found out it is a girl at the ultrasound.
The ultrasound is scheduled for Thursday.
She has had three ultrasounds so far.

entries.meaning: A party where friends give gifts to a woman before her baby arrives. ---
examples: Her sister is hosting the baby shower.
We got the stroller at the baby shower.
I have been to four baby showers this year.

entries.meaning: Time off work a mother takes after having a baby. ---
examples: She goes on maternity leave in June.
His company offers twelve weeks of maternity leave.
Maternity leave here is shorter than in most countries.

entries.meaning: Time off work a father takes after his child is born. ---
examples: He took a month of paternity leave.
Paternity leave is still rare at small firms.
They both used their paternity leave back to back.
entries.русский: отпуск отца по уходу за ребёнком

entries.meaning: The tube that connects an unborn baby to its mother. ---
examples: Her husband cut the umbilical cord.
The stump of the umbilical cord falls off in a week or two.
Umbilical cords are sometimes banked for stem cells.

entries.meaning: A baby born several weeks early. ---
examples: He was a preemie and spent a month in the hospital.
Preemie clothes are tiny.
The unit takes care of preemies from all over the state.
entries.contrast: A shortening of premature, but spelled with two e's: preemie.

entries.meaning: Incubator has 2 distinct senses.
examples: She spent three weeks in an incubator.
We could only touch him through the incubator.
Every incubator on the floor was full.
The eggs stay in the incubator for twenty-one days.
He built an incubator out of an old cooler.
The incubators have to hold a steady temperature.

senses.head: A heated enclosed crib that keeps a very small baby warm
examples: She spent three weeks in an incubator.
We could only touch him through the incubator.
Every incubator on the floor was full.

senses.head: A heated box that keeps eggs at the right temperature until they hatch
examples: The eggs stay in the incubator for twenty-one days.
He built an incubator out of an old cooler.
The incubators have to hold a steady temperature.

entries.meaning: The official document recording a person's birth. ---
examples: You need a birth certificate to get a passport.
His birth certificate has his name misspelled.
Ordering copies of birth certificates takes two weeks.

entries.meaning: An operation to deliver a baby through a cut in the mother's belly. ---
examples: After twenty hours they did a c-section.
Recovery from a c-section takes longer.
Both of her babies were c-sections.
entries.contrast: Short for cesarean section; the letter c is said by name, SEE.

entries.meaning: The visible curve of a pregnant woman's belly. ---
examples: She is finally showing a little baby bump.
That dress hides the baby bump completely.
The magazine had a whole page of celebrity baby bumps.

entries.meaning: A system in which a child lives temporarily with another family. ---
examples: He grew up in foster care.
The children were placed in foster care last spring.
Foster care is meant to be temporary.

entries.meaning: Money one parent pays the other for a child's expenses. ---
examples: He pays child support every month.
The judge raised the child support.
She is owed two years of child support.

entries.meaning: A divorced parent's legal right to spend time with a child. ---
examples: He has visitation every other weekend.
The visitation schedule is in the court order.
They went back to court over visitation.
entries.русский: право на встречи с ребёнком (после развода)

entries.meaning: The legal responsibility for a child who is not your own. ---
examples: Her aunt took guardianship of the two boys.
Guardianship has to be granted by a judge.
They are applying for guardianship this month.

entries.meaning: A regular meeting where small children play and parents talk. ---
examples: We joined a playgroup on our street.
The playgroup meets Tuesday mornings.
There are two playgroups at the community center.

entries.meaning: A school for children too young for kindergarten. ---
examples: She starts nursery school in the fall.
The nursery school is only three mornings a week.
Nursery schools fill up fast around here.

entries.meaning: A short traditional poem or song for young children. ---
examples: He can recite that nursery rhyme by heart.
The teacher sang a nursery rhyme to settle them down.
Old nursery rhymes are stranger than people remember.

entries.meaning: A story read or told to a child before sleep. ---
examples: One more bedtime story and then lights out.
Their dad makes up a new bedtime story every night.
We have read those bedtime stories a hundred times.

entries.meaning: The simple, sing-song way adults speak to babies. ---
examples: Grandpa slips into baby talk the second he sees her.
She is four now and still uses baby talk.
A little baby talk actually helps them learn words.

entries.meaning: A punishment in which a child is hit on the bottom. ---
examples: He got a spanking for that when he was little.
Most pediatricians advise against spanking.
Spankings were normal in her parents' day.

entries.meaning: The amount of time a child spends looking at a screen. ---
examples: We limit screen time to an hour a day.
Screen time went way up over the summer.
No screen time until the homework is done.

entries.meaning: Time a child spends playing. ---
examples: Playtime is over — go wash your hands.
Kids need unstructured playtime.
We get twenty minutes of playtime before bath.

entries.meaning: A set time when children are read to. ---
examples: The library has story time on Saturdays.
Story time is the best part of his day.
They sit on the rug for story time.

entries.meaning: A room in a house set aside for children to play in. ---
examples: The playroom is a disaster again.
They turned the basement into a playroom.
Some day cares have three separate playrooms.

entries.meaning: A program where children spend part of the summer away from home. ---
examples: She goes to summer camp in Maine every July.
Summer camp is where he learned to swim.
Sign-ups for summer camps open in February.

entries.meaning: A classroom activity where a child brings something in to talk about. ---
examples: He brought his turtle for show-and-tell.
Show-and-tell is on Fridays.
What are you taking to show-and-tell?

entries.meaning: The push a young person feels to act like their friends. ---
examples: Peer pressure is strongest in middle school.
We talk to our kids about peer pressure early.
He gave in to peer pressure and skipped class.

entries.meaning: A close, gentle hug, especially with a small child. ---
examples: She wanted one more cuddle before bed.
A quick cuddle fixed the whole meltdown.
Morning cuddles are the best part of the day.

entries.meaning: A ride on someone's back and shoulders. ---
examples: Give me a piggyback ride, Dad!
He carried her the last mile on a piggyback ride.
Piggyback rides are how we get through long walks.

entries.meaning: The care and upbringing a child receives, as opposed to inherited traits. ---
examples: It is the old argument about nature versus nurture.
Nurture shapes far more than people assume.
Both nature and nurture are at work here.

entries.meaning: Sandbox has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The kids spent an hour in the sandbox.
We covered the sandbox so the cats stay out.
Both sandboxes at the park need new sand.
Run the code in a sandbox first.
The bank gives developers a sandbox to test payments.
Nothing in the sandbox touches real customer data.

senses.head: A low box of sand where small children dig and build
examples: The kids spent an hour in the sandbox.
We covered the sandbox so the cats stay out.
Both sandboxes at the park need new sand.

senses.head: A separated area where new software can be tested safely
examples: Run the code in a sandbox first.
The bank gives developers a sandbox to test payments.
Nothing in the sandbox touches real customer data.

entries.contrast: American sandbox, British sandpit.

entries.meaning: A long board balanced in the middle so two children can go up and down. ---
examples: They rode the seesaw until dinner.
He is too heavy for the seesaw now.
The old metal seesaws were taken out years ago.
entries.contrast: Many Americans call it a teeter-totter instead.

entries.meaning: Swing has 3 distinct senses.
examples: Push me higher on the swing!
The baby swing has a bar across the front.
All four swings were taken.
He worked on his golf swing all summer.
She took a big swing and missed the ball.
The coach filmed each player's swing in slow motion.
There was a big swing toward the challenger in the final week.
Her mood swings worried her parents.
A ten-point swing in the polls decided the race.

senses.head: A seat hung on ropes or chains for a child to ride back and forth
examples: Push me higher on the swing!
The baby swing has a bar across the front.
All four swings were taken.

senses.head: A single act of swinging your arm, a bat, or a club at something
examples: He worked on his golf swing all summer.
She took a big swing and missed the ball.
The coach filmed each player's swing in slow motion.

senses.head: A clear shift from one position, mood, or result to another
examples: There was a big swing toward the challenger in the final week.
Her mood swings worried her parents.
A ten-point swing in the polls decided the race.

entries.русский: качели; замах, удар (в гольфе, бейсболе); сдвиг, резкая перемена
entries.contrast: Russian качели is plural, but one seat in English is a swing.

entries.meaning: A book of outline drawings for a child to color in. ---
examples: She filled a whole coloring book on the flight.
The restaurant hands out a coloring book and crayons.
We keep coloring books in the car.
entries.contrast: American spelling coloring; the British write colouring book.

entries.meaning: A wooden toy horse on curved runners that a child rides. ---
examples: Her grandfather built that rocking horse.
He rode the rocking horse until it tipped over.
Antique rocking horses sell for a fortune.

entries.meaning: A frame of bars for children to climb on. ---
examples: He fell off the jungle gym and scraped his knee.
They were hanging upside down from the jungle gym.
The new jungle gyms have soft mats underneath.
entries.contrast: The British call it a climbing frame.

entries.meaning: A shallow plastic pool for small children. ---
examples: We filled the kiddie pool in the backyard.
She sat in the kiddie pool all afternoon.
The store was out of kiddie pools by June.
entries.contrast: The British say paddling pool.

entries.meaning: An overhead ladder that children swing across hand over hand.
examples: She made it all the way across the monkey bars.
He got blisters from the monkey bars.
The monkey bars are the tallest thing on the playground.
entries.contrast: Plural only — nobody says "a monkey bar".
